whatTheyArgued: In his Locana on Anandavardhana's Dhvanyaloka (3.26) Abhinavagupta argues that shanta (the rasa of the fullness of the happiness of craving's cessation) is genuinely cognised (the snip, GRETIL e-text, verbatim). In the Abhinavabharati (commentary on the Natyasastra, not on disk) the secondary literature reports rasa as a depersonalised, universalised experience (sadharanikarana) of the cultivated spectator (sahrdaya), freed from ego and private associations.

scholarship.ref: Sreenivasa Rao, 'Abhinavabharati: an interpretation of Bharata's Natyasastra' (popular web essay, not peer-reviewed)
scholarship.supports: sahrdaya central; sadharanikarana lifts the spectator from the ego-bound to the general; Locana and Abhinavabharati are separate works
scholarship.disputes: weak source; I found no SEP/IEP entry in the search and did not read a peer-reviewed work in full (a JIP 2016 article and an SJSU paper appeared in search results but I did not open them)

ourUse: pathos.js: a pathos finding is refused without a declared experiencer ('for whom'); the re-ground is named 'shanta'. Header discloses the namesake is never asserted as measurement.

bends.theirs: The verified snip and the pathos.js epigraph come from the Locana on the Dhvanyaloka, a different work. The Abhinavabharati is not on disk and nothing in the code cites it.

bends.ours: 'it has a for whom, never a view from nowhere': a named, particular experiencer is mandatory.
bends.theirs: The sahrdaya is central, but rasa is experienced through sadharanikarana, depersonalised and not tied to a particular person's private situation. Our declared-experiencer rule is a design law, not his claim, and nearly inverts the universalisation emphasis.

bends.ours: The re-ground is called 'shanta', the culminating state after pathemata are released.
bends.theirs: Shanta is a rasa whose existence Abhinava defends; it is not a mechanism for conceding and reopening a ground. The header already says the namesake is disclosed, not asserted.

fix: compendium work: 'Kashmir Shaiva aesthetician. In his Locana on the Dhvanyaloka (3.26) he defends shanta, the rasa of craving's cessation, as truly cognised; in the Abhinavabharati rasa is the cultivated spectator's depersonalised experience. Our code takes only the name for the re-ground and adds its own rule that a feeling needs a declared experiencer.'
compendium source/credit: 'Locana on Dhvanyaloka 3.26 (and, by report, Abhinavabharati)'; drop 'never a view from nowhere' as his claim
pathos.js header: keep the disclosure; say 'for whom' is our rule, set against his universalisation
